title: Louise de Marillac and the Daughters of Charity
hookLine: sisters without a cloister: the streets and hospitals were their convent

lines: A COUNTRY GIRL AT THE DOOR.
A WIDOW WHO WAS TURNED AWAY.
cards: A young woman from the countryside arrives in Paris with a small bundle and one wish: to care for the poor and the sick. She has heard that a lady here trains girls for that work.

The lady who takes her in is a widow of noble birth, anxious by temperament, who once wanted to be a nun and was turned away. Together they're about to build a community of women who serve God with no convent walls.
Today, Louise de Marillac and the Daughters of Charity.

teach.b: First, Louise. Born to a noble family but outside marriage, she grew up never quite belonging. She asked to enter a strict convent and was refused, partly for her health.
She married, had a son, nursed her husband through a long illness, and was left a widow, troubled by doubt and worry. Second, Vincent.
Vincent de Paul became her spiritual director and gave her work: visiting the charity groups he had started in the parishes, checking their accounts, encouraging the volunteers. She was good at it.
She saw what the noble ladies couldn't do themselves: the daily, dirty, tiring care of the sick at home. Third, the Daughters.

Country girls began coming to serve, and Louise took them into her own house to train them. That was the beginning of the Daughters of Charity. To keep them free for the streets, they weren't set up as an enclosed order.

Vincent put it to them in words they remembered, paraphrased here: your convent is the houses of the sick, your cell a rented room, your chapel the parish church, your cloister the streets of the city. Fourth, the work.
They nursed in hospitals, cared for abandoned babies, visited prisoners, taught poor girls.

teach.h: GO, AND DO THOU IN LIKE MANNER.
teach.b: When a lawyer in Luke's Gospel asks who his neighbor is, Jesus tells the story of the Samaritan on the road and ends, in the Douay-Rheims: "Go, and do thou in like manner." The Daughters took that road as their cloister.

how: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Louise de Marillac, and the Daughters of Charity still work in hospitals, schools and among the poor; some Catholic social workers and nurses look to her as a patron.

practice: Think of the streets you'll walk or drive today and who is out there: someone asking for change at a corner, a person sleeping in a doorway, a delivery worker in the rain.

Pick one, and ask what a small act of service might look like: a greeting, a bottle of water, a meal, a real look in the eye. If you pray, pray for that person by name or by face; if not, simply hold them, and plan the small act.
